draft.title: Buddhist environmental ethics
card: Buddhists teach that all things exist in relation to one another and depend on causes and conditions. Humans, animals and the natural world are linked, so harm to one part can affect others.
Buddhists aim to show compassion (karuna) to all living beings, not only to humans. This includes the animals and plants that share the natural world.
The first precept, to avoid harming living beings, is applied by many Buddhists to the damage that pollution, waste and habitat loss can cause.

Together, these ideas lead many Buddhists to care for the environment, such as by living simply, protecting forests or taking part in conservation. Buddhist teachers and communities may apply them in different ways.
draft.remember: Many Buddhists care for the environment because all life is linked and compassion reaches all living beings.

a.q: Which Buddhist idea best explains why harm to a river could be seen as harm to the people and animals that depend on it?
opts: Interdependence, because all things are linked
Impermanence, because all things are always changing
Authority, because rivers are owned by the sangha
Reward, because protecting nature earns a better life
a.why: Interdependence teaches that humans, animals and nature depend on one another, so harm to a river reaches those who rely on it. Impermanence is tempting, but it is about change, not about how living things are linked.
a.clue: Which idea is about things being connected?

b.q: A Buddhist community in Victoria replants a bushfire-damaged forest and explains that it wants to avoid harming the animals that live there. Which Buddhist teaching does this reason rely on most directly?
opts: Compassion for all living beings, not only humans
Compassion for fellow humans in the community
Interdependence, which says humans must own the land
The view that nature cannot be harmed by people
b.why: The community's stated aim is to avoid harming animals, which reflects compassion that reaches all living beings. The option about fellow humans is tempting, but it leaves out the animals, and Buddhist compassion is not limited to humans.
b.clue: Look at who the community says it wants to protect.

a.best: Interdependence, because all things are linked

b.best: Compassion for all living beings, not only humans

problems.detail: The card says compassion (karuna) to all living beings 'includes the animals and plants'. In most Buddhist teaching, karuna is directed at sentient beings, and plants are generally not counted as sentient beings. Some East Asian traditions do extend Buddha-nature to plants, so the claim needs qualifying, for example 'some Buddhists extend this care to plants'.

check.summary: Both questions work and have one clear right answer. The card overstates that Buddhist compassion (karuna) includes plants, which is contested because plants are usually not treated as sentient beings.

proposal.title: Buddhist environmental ethics
card: Buddhists teach that all things exist in relation to one another and depend on causes and conditions. Humans, animals and the natural world are linked, so harm to one part can affect others.
Compassion (karuna) is the wish to free all sentient beings, those that can feel and suffer, from suffering. It reaches animals as well as humans, and some Buddhists extend this care to plants.
The first precept, to avoid harming living beings, is applied by many Buddhists to the damage that pollution, waste and habitat loss can cause.

Together, these ideas lead many Buddhists to care for the environment, such as by living simply, protecting forests or taking part in conservation. Buddhist teachers and communities may apply them in different ways.
proposal.remember: Many Buddhists care for the environment because all life is linked and compassion reaches beyond humans.

a.q: Which Buddhist idea best explains why harm to a river could be seen as harm to the people and animals that depend on it?
opts: Interdependence, because all things are linked
Impermanence, because all things are always changing
Non-self, because no being has a fixed, lasting self
Rebirth, because beings are born again after death
a.why: Interdependence teaches that humans, animals and nature depend on one another, so harm to a river reaches those who rely on it. Impermanence is tempting, but it is about change, not about how living things are linked.
a.clue: Which idea is about things being connected?

b.q: A Buddhist community in Victoria replants a bushfire-damaged forest. It says it wants to ease the suffering of the animals that lost their homes. Which teaching does this reason rely on most directly?
opts: Compassion for all sentient beings, not only humans
Compassion for fellow humans in the local community
Interdependence, which says humans must own the land
The view that animals cannot truly feel or suffer
b.why: The community wants to ease the suffering of animals, which reflects compassion for all sentient beings. The option about fellow humans is tempting, but it leaves out the animals, and Buddhist compassion is not limited to humans.
b.clue: Look at whose suffering the community wants to ease.
